terms.label: IPTV
terms.short: TV delivered over the internet instead of an antenna or cable box.
terms.longer: ChannelForge does not supply TV. It organizes playlists and guides you already have.

terms.label: Provider
terms.short: The company or service that gives you channels.
terms.longer: One provider can give you several sources, such as a playlist and a guide.

terms.label: Source
terms.short: One playlist or guide input, from a provider or a local file.
terms.longer: A source is a single file or address. A provider is who it came from.

terms.label: M3U playlist
terms.short: A file or address listing channel names and where to stream each one.
terms.longer: It has no schedule. The schedule comes from the guide.

terms.label: Stream URL
terms.short: The web address a player opens to play one channel.
terms.longer: Treat it as private. It may carry your login, so ChannelForge never shows it.

terms.label: Channel
terms.short: A named TV channel, such as a news or sports channel.
terms.longer: A channel is what you pick. A stream is the video that plays when you pick it.

terms.label: Channel ID
terms.short: A short name that marks one channel so a guide can match it.
terms.longer: The playlist and the guide must use the same ID for the match to work.

terms.label: tvg-id
terms.short: The channel ID field inside an M3U playlist line.
terms.longer: It is the playlist side of the match. The guide side is the channel ID in the XMLTV file.

terms.label: Group
terms.short: A label that sorts channels into sets, such as News or Sports.
terms.longer: Groups only organize the list. They do not change what plays.

terms.label: XMLTV guide
terms.short: Schedule data that says what is playing on each channel and when.
terms.longer: It is a file in the XMLTV format. It has schedules, not video.

terms.label: EPG
terms.short: Electronic program guide: the on-screen schedule in a player.
terms.longer: The EPG is what you see. XMLTV is a common file that feeds it.

terms.label: Programme
terms.short: One show or event in the guide, with a start and an end time.
terms.longer: The guide spells it programme, so ChannelForge uses that word for guide entries.

terms.label: Timeshift
terms.short: Pausing or rewinding live TV.
terms.longer: It needs support from the provider or player. It is not the same as buffering.

terms.label: Catch-up
terms.short: Watching a show that already aired.
terms.longer: Only some providers offer it, and only for a limited time.

terms.label: Proxy
terms.short: A middle step that passes streams along instead of sending you straight to the provider.
terms.longer: It can hide the provider address, but it adds a step that can fail.

terms.label: Buffering
terms.short: Video that stops while the player loads more data.
terms.longer: It is a short wait for data. It is not rewind or pause.

terms.label: Bitrate
terms.short: How much data per second a video uses.
terms.longer: A higher bitrate can look better but needs a faster connection.

terms.label: Codec
terms.short: The method used to shrink video or audio so it can be sent.
terms.longer: Common ones are H.264 and AAC. A player must understand the codec to play it.

terms.label: Container
terms.short: The file or stream wrapper that holds video and audio together.
terms.longer: Examples are MP4 and MPEG-TS. The container is not the codec.

terms.label: Transcoding
terms.short: Converting video to a new format so a device can play it.
terms.longer: It uses a lot of computer power and can lower quality.

terms.label: Remuxing
terms.short: Moving video into a new container without changing the video itself.
terms.longer: It is fast and keeps quality, unlike transcoding.

terms.label: Direct play
terms.short: Playing a stream as it is, with no conversion.
terms.longer: It is the lightest option, but the device must support the format.

terms.label: Resolution
terms.short: The picture size, such as 1920 by 1080.
terms.longer: More pixels give a sharper picture and use more data.

terms.label: Refresh interval
terms.short: How often ChannelForge fetches a source again.
terms.longer: Shorter intervals stay current but ask the provider more often.

terms.label: Fallback guide data
terms.short: Basic schedule entries used when a channel has no real guide data.
terms.longer: They keep the channel in the list. They are placeholders, not real schedules.

terms.label: Candidate lineup
terms.short: A proposed lineup that you have not accepted yet.
terms.longer: It cannot replace your current lineup by itself.

terms.label: Last-known-good
terms.short: The newest result that passed checks, kept when a later refresh fails.
terms.longer: It lets you keep a working lineup while you fix the problem.
